how-it-works.title: How it works
how-it-works.lead: Claude Code lives on your server; each of your computers is a pair of hands for it.
how-it-works.words: architecture server execution channel ssh tunnel upload how

list1: **Sessions and memory are on the server**: close the client, switch computers or pick up your phone, and you carry on with the same session.
**Files and commands are on your computer**: over an encrypted channel, Claude reads and writes files and runs commands on your computer. Your project doesn’t move to the server and isn’t uploaded.
**Your computer connects out**: no public IP and no inbound port. Once it disconnects, that connection’s channel and temporary keys are void.

tip1.title: ssh device-… in the steps is normal
tip1.text: That is Claude working on your computer: `device` is the one the session is on, `device-<name>` your other computers that are online.

note1.title: Now and then it creates files on the server
note1.text: When the project is on your computer but a path in the steps starts with `/data/state/native/`, Claude is working on the server. Tell it “do it on my computer instead”.

tip2.title: The server is a place to work too
tip2.text: The server’s own environment is there to use too: a plain session started in a browser or on a phone runs on the server, and Claude may keep files or prepare work there. When the project is on your computer, though, the change has to end up on that computer; left on the server, it isn’t done.

sessions.title: Projects and sessions
sessions.lead: A project is a folder on a computer; a session is a conversation, its context and memory kept on the server.
sessions.words: project folder fork edit and resend pin rename export remove plain session recent

list1: **Projects**: click + next to “Projects” in the left column to add one; you can rename it. Starting a session in `ccdt` also adds its folder as a project.

**Plain sessions**: “New session” gives you one. It belongs to no project and is listed under “Recent”. Its working folder is under “Documents\CC Desk Tunnel” unless you change it in [General](settings:general).
list2: **The same projects everywhere**: the server keeps the list of projects, so every computer, browser and `ccdt` sees the same one, offline computers’ projects included; a new name shows everywhere.
**Removing a project** only takes it off the list. The folder, its sessions and the project’s memory stay; its sessions become plain sessions. Add the same folder again and they’re all back.
list3: **Moving elsewhere**: click the project tag above the input box to move the session to another project or to another computer that is online. A session that has been used keeps the memory of the project it came from.
**Edit and resend**: hover over a message of yours and click “Edit and resend” to fork a new session from just before it. The original session stays; changes already made to files are not undone.

tip1.title: Right-click a session
tip1.text: Pin, rename, export to Markdown and open in `ccdt` are in the session’s context menu (or ⋯). An export can hold only the questions and answers, or only the last few turns, which is much quicker for a long session.

conversation.title: Tips for talking to Claude
conversation.lead: Talk as you would to Claude Code; a few handy extras come on top.
conversation.words: add instruction stop continue slash command skills attachment screenshot image paste model effort shortcuts find

list1: **Talk while it works**: send a message while Claude is busy and it joins the turn under way, to steer or add something.
**Stop and continue**: stop the turn at the bottom right of the input box. After stopping or a dropped connection, click “Continue” to carry on without writing anything more.
**The command menu**: type `/` or `\` for compacting the context, and for Claude Code’s commands and skills.
**Give it files and screenshots**: click +, or drag them in or paste them. The message holds the file’s path on your computer, and Claude reads it there; nothing is uploaded.
**A plan first for big changes**: switch to [Plan mode](#approval). It writes a plan, and once you have edited and approved it, it gets to work.
**Model and effort**: switch them below the input box; they apply to this session only.

note1.title: The status dot stops and says how long nothing has come
note1.text: It only means no new messages arrived in that time, not that something went wrong; long commands often do this.

blocks.p2: For longer work Claude lists the steps first and ticks them off as it goes. While some are left, the list shows above the message box; click its title to fold it. `ccdt status` and ACP editors show the progress too. Newer models don’t keep a list on their own, so this server turns it on for them; turn off “Task list” in the CLI settings if you don’t want it.

items.text: Add a small feature to this project in steps: read the code, change it, then run it to check. Track the steps in a task list

approval.title: Approval modes
approval.lead: Whether Claude asks you before it acts. Switch at the bottom left of the input box.
approval.words: approval permission allow deny auto manual plan accept edits bypass safety check

list1: **Auto approval most of the time** (the default): Claude Code weighs the risk itself and asks you only when it needs to.

**Auto approval when nobody is watching**: the other modes stop at an approval and wait for someone. Auto approval asks now and then too; with [“Deny instead of asking”](#unattended#deny) it never stops.
**Switching**: click the bottom left of the input box, or press [[cycleMode]] to go through the modes.
**When it asks you**, an approval card appears in the conversation, saying what it wants to do and on which computer. You can approve from your phone or a browser too.
blocks.approval: The approval card: allow it once, or deny it and say why.

note1.title: A “Claude Code safety check” asks in every mode
note1.text: Some actions always need your confirmation by Claude Code’s own safety checks, in Auto approval and Bypass permissions too. Such cards say “Claude Code safety check”.

warn1.title: Bypass permissions
warn1.text: Asks about nothing except the safety checks, including deleting files and running any command on your computer. It isn’t offered until you allow it in [General](settings:general); use it only on a test machine or a virtual machine.

quota.title: Quota and usage
quota.lead: See the 5-hour and weekly quota in “Account and quota”, or show it beside the input box.
quota.words: quota usage 5-hour weekly limit cost token call log save

list1: **Use `ccdt` when the 5-hour quota is tight**: the desktop client runs through the official Agent SDK. Community measurements put the share of the same use counted against the 5-hour quota at about twice that of the interactive CLI; the weekly quota is not affected. See [how ccdt is best used](#ccdt).

**Quota beside the input box**: turn it on in [Appearance](settings:appearance). It shows the 5-hour and the whole account’s weekly use; when the model in use has a weekly limit of its own that is further used (such as Fable on Max), that one is shown instead, named after the model.
**Fast mode doesn’t use the plan’s quota**: on a subscription it is charged straight to extra usage; see [Fast mode](#model-settings#fast).
**The call log**: each request’s model, tokens and equivalent cost; the amounts are estimated at API prices, not a bill.
**The quota is empty**: it comes from a run of Claude Code; send a message, or refresh on the account page.

account.title: Claude account
account.lead: The account signs in on the server; every computer, browser and ccdt shares it.

list1: **Ordinary sign-in**: open the official authorization page and paste back the code it gives.
**Setup token**: made by the server, or paste one you have; this way the email, subscription type and full quota may not show.
**Signing out** removes the token kept on the server; the session history stays. Running the official `/logout` in `ccdt` does not remove it.

context.title: Cache and compaction
context.lead: Each turn, Claude reads the whole session again. With a cache that is cheap; once the cache expires or is broken, the next turn reads it all at full price. Several settings revolve around this.
context.words: cache expiry expire compaction compact context idle 1 hour 5 minutes ttl prompt cache auto compaction window cache read cache write save

blocks.p1: With every message, Claude Code sends the system prompt, the instruction files, every earlier message and tool result again in full. The first part, the same as in the turn before, is read from the cache at about a tenth of the price of ordinary input; without the cache, all of it is processed and written again. The longer the session, the slower and dearer the first turn after you come back.
list1: **The cache expires**: after 5 minutes or 1 hour with no new request since the last. Every request starts the clock again.

**These break the cache**: changing the model, turning fast mode on or off, adding or removing an MCP server, compaction. On older models, changing the effort does too. The model is best chosen at the start of a session.
**Editing instruction files doesn’t**, but a session under way doesn’t see the change either; it takes effect after compaction or in a new session.
blocks.p2: A 1-hour cache lasts through a gap like lunch or a meeting, at the cost of dearer writes: at API prices, writing a 1-hour cache costs 2 times ordinary input, a 5-minute one 1.25 times. For a conversation that never pauses for more than 5 minutes, 1 hour only costs more.

head: Requests
Default
rows: The main conversation on a subscription
Subagents, workflows, compaction and the like on a subscription

note1.title: Once the plan’s quota is used up, the default becomes 5 minutes
note1.text: Past the plan’s quota, paying with extra usage (usage credits), Claude Code moves the main conversation to a 5-minute cache. To keep 1 hour then too, set [“Prompt cache lifetime”](settings:claude) to 1 hour explicitly.

blocks.p3: “Prompt cache lifetime for subtasks” covers the requests outside the main conversation, such as subagents, workflows and compaction; it is usually best left as it is.
blocks.idle: Compacting before you’re away too long
blocks.p4: Compaction replaces a long session with a summary, and from then on each turn reads only the summary. Compacting while the cache is still there reads the cache, which is cheap; compacting after it expires reads everything at full price. Auto compaction in [Context and cache](settings:context) does this for you before the cache expires: once a session has been idle for the time set, the server compacts it on its own, with neither your computer nor the client needing to be online.
list2: **Off by default**; turn it on in [Context and cache](settings:context).
**Only for sessions with a 1-hour cache.** With “Prompt cache lifetime” at 5 minutes, or signed in with an API key, the cache expires before compaction could come, so it doesn’t happen.
**Compact after idle for**: 50 minutes by default. The nearer to 60 minutes, the less likely you come back meanwhile and the compaction is wasted, but the less margin it has.
**Context at least**: a small session isn’t dear even read at full price, and isn’t worth compacting.
**Compaction is a real request**: it counts against the quota, and the summary loses detail. If you’re only away a short while, you don’t need it.

**When it is off**, the session reminds you as the cache is about to expire, and you decide whether to compact. For a long session whose cache has already expired, switch to a cheaper model before compacting, or just start a new one.
Sessions in `ccdt` are compacted by Claude Code itself: with the switch and context size set here, at a fixed time of about 54 minutes.
blocks.window: Compaction when the context is nearly full
blocks.p5: This is something else: when a session grows close to the model’s context limit, Claude Code compacts it on its own and carries on. “Auto-compact context” in [CLI settings](settings:claude) controls it; it is on by default.
list3: **Auto-compact window**: the context size at which it compacts, 100K at least. Smaller means less to read each turn, cheaper and a more focused Claude, at the cost of compacting more often and losing detail. For models with a 1M context, 300K to 500K keeps a session from growing dearer the longer it goes.
**Prepare compaction summaries ahead**: the summary is worked out in the background first, so compaction takes less waiting.
**With “Auto-compact context” off**, a full context can only be compacted by hand or left for a new session; idle compaction in `ccdt` goes off with it.

tip1.title: Pick the moment to compact by hand
tip1.text: Typing `/compact` between two pieces of work is better than being compacted halfway through one. When it has gone the wrong way and you’d drop the whole stretch, a new session is cleaner than compaction.

blocks.numbers: Reading the cache from the figures
blocks.p6: The reply summary and the session bar can show “Cache read” and “Cache write”; choose them in [Appearance](settings:appearance).
list4: **Reads far above writes**: the cache is working.
**One turn with a very large write**: the cache was just broken, usually by being away too long, a model change or a compaction.
**Large writes every turn**: something keeps breaking the cache, such as switching models back and forth.

unattended.title: Letting tasks finish on their own
unattended.lead: Long tasks, night tasks and scheduled tasks suffer most from stopping at one question and waiting. With a few settings working together, a task can go all the way.

head: Stops at
What to do
rows: Use **Auto approval**, and turn on [“Deny instead of asking”](#unattended#deny)
Say in the task not to ask questions; see [below](#unattended#question)
Your computer sleeps or drops off
The computer doesn’t go to sleep on its own while the client is open; a task stops only after 5 minutes offline

list1: Turned on in [CLI settings](settings:claude), a call that needs your approval no longer waits for you but is denied at once; Claude knows it was denied and tries another way, or tells you at the end.

**Use it with Auto approval**: allow rules and Auto approval decide first as usual, Auto approval lets through what it takes to be safe, and only the rest is denied. In Manual approval almost nothing gets done.
**It applies to every session**, `ccdt` included. Turn it off once the task is done, or it won’t ask you even while you’re there.
blocks.question: A question from Claude
blocks.p1: In the desktop client, a question card waits for your answer. For a task nobody watches, say in the prompt how far to go and not to ask questions:

items.text: Update every outdated passage in the docs folder, and stop only when done. Don’t ask me along the way; where unsure, take the most cautious choice, and list those places for me at the end.

blocks.p2: In `ccdt` there is also the CLI setting “When a question goes unanswered”: after a while it carries on by itself with the options chosen.
blocks.p3: In the desktop client, the turn ends when the quota runs out. To have it carry on after the quota resets, tell Claude, and it sets up a [scheduled task](#schedules):

items.text: Once the quota resets, send “carry on with the task” in this session

blocks.p4: See when it resets in [Account and quota](settings:account). `ccdt` needs none of this: the CLI setting “Carry on after the quota runs out” is on by default, and the terminal waits for the reset and carries on.

steps1.title: Choose Auto approval
steps1.text: Switch at the bottom left of the input box.

steps1.title: Turn on “Deny instead of asking”
steps1.text: Turn it off again when done.

steps1.title: Say in the prompt where to end
steps1.text: How far to go, what to do when unsure, and what to report at the end.

steps1.title: Keep the client open
steps1.text: Closing the window only sends it to the tray. Keep the notifications of done and failed tasks on, to see the result as soon as you’re back.

model-settings.title: Thinking, speed and fallback models
model-settings.lead: These decide how deeply Claude thinks, how fast it goes and what happens when the main model is busy. The two most misunderstood points: turning “Thinking” off does nothing on newer models, and fast mode costs extra on a subscription.
model-settings.words: thinking effort show thinking fast mode extra usage usage credits fallback model safety block switch models

list1: **Thinking** matters only on older models. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and the Fable models always think, and do even with it off.
**For less thinking and more speed**, lower the effort under “Model and effort” at the bottom left of the input box; each session can differ.

**Show thinking** only decides whether you see a summary of the thinking; how much Claude thinks and the quota it uses stay the same. Turn it on to see why it does something: the conversation gains thinking you can expand.
list2: Output is clearly faster, and each token dearer. Only some models support it, such as Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2.
**On a subscription it doesn’t use the plan’s quota**: fast mode is charged straight to extra usage (usage credits), even with plan quota left; without extra usage turned on it can’t be used.
Turning it on or off midway makes the next turn read everything at full price. If you use it, turn it on at the start of a session.
When the extra usage is used up, it falls back to normal speed and carries on.
blocks.fallback: When the main model is busy or failing
list3: **Fallback models**: when the main model is overloaded or unavailable, it moves to the next in order to finish the turn; the next message tries the main model first again. Without any, it only retries the main model, and reports an error if that still fails.
Up to 3, separated by commas, such as `sonnet, haiku`. A turn moved to another model has no cache and costs somewhat more.

**Switch models on a safety block**: Claude Code’s safety checks now and then stop a request, and by default it carries on with another model. With it off, the turn ends with an error in the desktop client; `ccdt` pauses and lets you choose between switching models and changing the prompt.

memory.title: Memory and instructions
memory.lead: Each of Claude’s sessions starts blank, and learns your habits from instruction files and auto memory. Where they are decides what Claude remembers.
memory.words: memory auto memory CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md global instructions instruction file remember forget reply language attribution git commit PR

head: Where it is, and who reads it
rows: The user-level `CLAUDE.md` on the server, read at the start of every session. Edit it in [Global instructions](settings:instructions)
In the project folder on your computer. Claude Code is on the server and **doesn’t read them on its own**; [synced](#memory#project) to the server, they are read
Notes Claude keeps itself, saved on the server by project

blocks.project: Having Claude read your project’s instructions
blocks.p0: There are two ways. One is to sync them to the server: Claude Code reads the server’s copy, from the next message on.
list0: Choose “Sync project instructions and skills” in the session’s context menu (or ⋯), the project’s menu in the sidebar, after `/` in the input box, or in [Global instructions](settings:instructions).
It syncs `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, and the rules, skills, commands and agents under `.claude/`. The project’s settings and MCP servers are not synced: they would run on the server.
Both sides are compared first: new files are copied; ones that differ can be replaced, or handed to Claude with a prompt to compare and merge them. It works from the server back to the computer too.
blocks.p1: The other is to have each session read them, with a line in the global instructions:

code1.label: Put in the global instructions
code1.text: On entering a project, first read CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md at the project’s root (if there is one), and work by what it says.

list1: As it works, Claude notes the ways you corrected it, your preferences and how the project stands, and reads them at the start of the next session.

**Kept by project**: the sessions of one project folder on one computer share them; each plain session has its own. A session that has been used and is moved to another project keeps the memory of the project it came from.
To have it remember something, say “remember: …”; if it got something wrong, say “delete what you remember about …”.
“Tidy memory in the background” merges and tidies the memory there is while idle. With “Auto memory” off, Claude neither reads nor writes these notes.

note1.title: When a change to the instructions applies
note1.text: Instructions are read once, at the start of a session. A session under way doesn’t see a change; it applies after compaction or in a new session.

list2: **Reply language** goes to Claude as it is, as a request to “always reply in this language”; any name of the language will do, such as `japanese` or `Français`.
**Attribution in commits and PRs**: by default Claude’s attribution is added to commit messages and PR descriptions; choose “No attribution” to leave it out.

**Built-in commit and PR instructions**: the official ways of committing and opening PRs, and the state of the repository, that come with it. If you have conventions of your own, turn it off and write them into the global instructions.

news.p0: Sync a project’s instructions and skills to the server

execution.title: Running on your computer
execution.lead: Claude reads files, changes files and runs builds on your computer by running commands over the execution channel. The shell, the command output limit and the connection waits decide how smoothly that goes.
execution.words: shell powershell git bash command output truncated limit tool search mcp artifact connection wait timeout domain controller security software

list1: Unset, Claude picks one for the task. Chosen, it is only a preference: when a task clearly suits the other, it still switches.
**PowerShell**: smoother for working on Windows itself (services, the registry, processes).
**Git Bash**: if you know Linux commands, or the project is mostly shell scripts. Install Git for Windows first; it can be chosen after reconnecting.
PowerShell 7 comes with the client. This is set on each Windows computer separately, and applies from each session’s next message.
list2: When a command’s output goes over the limit, the rest is saved to a file, and Claude sees only the start and where the file is, to read it next.
Raise it when build logs and test results are often truncated and Claude keeps going back to the files. The higher the limit, the more context each output takes and the faster a session grows.
4K to 128K characters; 30K by default.
list3: **Tool search**: the tools’ descriptions are no longer all sent each time but looked up when needed. With many MCP tools connected this saves a lot of context. On by default for official accounts; third-party endpoints must support it.
**Artifact pages**: Claude can publish documents, plans and charts as pages on claude.ai that only you can see, to share when you want. Turn it off if you don’t use it.
list4: Connecting to the server, starting this computer’s SSH service, and the execution channel getting ready each have a time limit, and are retried when it passes.

**Most computers need no change.** With a company domain account that can’t reach its domain controller, or security software that scans slowly, the second step takes longer; raise it only if it keeps timing out.
“Execution channel ready” is at least 35 seconds more than “Local SSH service starts”. It affects only this computer.

permissions.title: Permission switches
permissions.lead: Whether you are asked is up to the approval mode. The switches below each cover a small part, and it is easy to think they do more.
permissions.words: permission bypass working directory write files checkpoint rewind undo block

blocks.p1: Only once it is turned on in [General](settings:general) does “Bypass permissions” appear among the approval modes, on this computer only. With it, nothing is asked except Claude Code’s safety checks, including deleting files and running any command on your computer. Use it only on a test machine or a virtual machine.
list1: It limits Claude Code’s tools for writing and editing files, and these tools work only on **files on the server**.
**It doesn’t stop changes to your computer**: Claude changes files on your computer by running commands, which this switch doesn’t limit. Against unwanted changes, rely on the approval mode.
With it on, these tools can’t change Claude Code’s own settings files either; Claude’s memory and plan files are not affected.
blocks.p2: Snapshots taken before edits, for `/rewind` to undo. Of use only in `ccdt`, and covering only files on the server changed with the editing tools. For the projects on your computer, Git is more reliable.

note1.title: Two more
note1.text: For “Deny instead of asking”, see [Letting tasks finish on their own](#unattended#deny). Claude Code’s safety checks ask in every mode; see [Approval modes](#approval).

plugins.title: Plugins
plugins.lead: When something happens, the server runs a plugin’s command: push approvals, questions and finished tasks to your phone, or into a system of your own.
plugins.words: plugins notifications push hooks events ntfy Telegram DingTalk Feishu WeCom webhook

blocks.p1: A plugin is a folder in the `plugins` folder of the server’s data directory, written as a Claude Code plugin is. It works a moment after it is put there, with no restart.

items.text: Write a plugin that pushes to my Telegram when you wait for my approval or finish a turn
items.note: Claude writes it as “Developing plugins” says and puts it on the server; fill in the bot token in the settings and it works.

items.text: Look at the plugin log and tell me why the last push didn’t go out

steps1.title: Install
steps1.text: Have Claude write it, or put a plugin’s folder in `plugins` in the server’s data directory (`/data/state/plugins` in the container of a Docker deployment).

steps1.title: Set up
steps1.text: Open it in Settings → Plugins and fill in what it asks for, such as where to push or a token.

steps1.title: Try
steps1.text: Click an event it handles to run it once on an example; the result is in the log below.

head: Event
When
rows: Waiting for approval, including of a plan
Claude asks a question and waits for your answer
A `ccdt` terminal waits for you to confirm
One of the waits above was answered, or the run ended
The turn is answered; only background tasks are left
A turn ended: completed, failed or stopped
A computer went online or offline

warn1.title: Install only plugins you trust
warn1.text: A plugin can do what the server can: read the server’s credentials and run commands on your computers that are online. Install only ones you wrote, Claude wrote for you, or that come from a source you trust.

plugin-dev.title: Developing plugins
plugin-dev.lead: Written as a Claude Code plugin is: a folder and a hooks.json, with its settings declared in plugin.json.
plugin-dev.words: developing plugins hooks.json plugin.json userConfig matcher CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION environment variables spec

blocks.p1: A plugin is a folder in the server’s `plugins` folder, and the folder’s name is its id (lowercase letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-`). Changes take effect a moment later.

code1.label: Layout
code1.text:
<id>/
├── .claude-plugin/plugin.json   name, version, settings (optional)
├── hooks/hooks.json             which command each event runs
└── notify.mjs                   the plugin’s own program

code2.label: Run your own script when a turn completes or fails

list1: `type` is `command` only. With `args`, `command` is started directly; without, it is given to the shell.
`matcher` is written as in Claude Code: none or `*` matches all, `a|b` lists names, anything else is a regular expression. The field it is held against is in the table below.
`timeout` is in seconds, 60 by default and 600 at most; on it, the command ends with what it started. At most 8 commands run at once.

The event is one JSON object on standard input. `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` is the plugin’s folder, `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA` a folder for its state, and each setting is `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>`, the key in capitals. `args` may hold `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` and `${user_config.KEY}`.
What a command prints goes to the log, with secrets that appear as they are replaced by `***`.
list2: `type` is `string`, `number` or `boolean`; `title` is required, and `description`, `required` and `default` are optional. Text may have `options` (a list to pick from), a number `min` and `max`.
A `sensitive` value can’t be read back once saved; only the commands get it. While a required setting has no value, the plugin doesn’t run.
The settings page draws its form from these declarations; the plugin’s code takes no part in drawing it.

head: Event
More fields (what matcher is held against in brackets)

list3: Every event has `version`, `hook_event_name` and `timestamp`; a session’s event also has `session_id`, `session_title`, `project_path`, `run_id`, `device` (`id`, `name`, `platform`), `model`, `permission_mode`, `context` and `quota`. A field with no value is left out.
Events hold nothing of the conversation, nor tools’ input and output. `reason` and `message` are words for people: don’t act on their text.
The spec only grows: events and fields added later leave existing plugins working, and unknown events and fields are ignored.

background.title: Background and notifications
background.lead: Closing the window doesn’t disconnect; you’re told when a task is done or needs you.
background.words: tray background notification disconnect reconnect sleep several servers window

list1: **Closing the window only sends it to the tray**: the connection and tasks go on; right-click the tray icon and choose “Quit” to disconnect. While connected, the computer doesn’t go to sleep on its own.
**Notifications**: while the window is not in front, you’re told of tasks done or failed, approvals waiting and questions from Claude; each kind can be turned off on its own.

**A dropped network needs nothing from you**: the client reconnects by itself, and tasks go on on the server. A task stops only after the computer has been offline for 5 minutes; when back, click “Continue”.
**Several servers**: one window each, with their own credentials, drafts and scheduled tasks.

upgrade.title: Upgrading
upgrade.lead: The client, ccdt and the server must be of the same version; one click in the client upgrades them, with no signing in to the server.
upgrade.words: upgrade update version mismatch new version

steps1.title: Seeing a new version
steps1.text: A download icon appears on the left; or check in “About and updates”.

steps1.title: Upgrade the server first
steps1.text: It reconnects on its own after about a minute. You’re told if sessions are running.

steps1.title: Then the client
steps1.text: On Windows it downloads and installs in the client, or from GitHub while the server has no installer ready yet; on macOS and Linux, download and install it again.

list1: The `ccdt` that comes with the desktop client upgrades with it; one installed on its own runs `ccdt upgrade`.

safety.title: Safety notes
safety.lead: The server can run commands as you on every computer connected to it. It must be a machine you control and trust.
safety.words: safety security credential token leak sandbox risk privacy

list1: **The service token is full control**: don’t take screenshots of it or paste it into chats and issues. If it leaks, run `sudo cc-desk-tunnel token` on the server to change it.
**It’s not a sandbox**: Claude can reach everything your user can on that computer, and can connect to your other computers that are online.
**Data leaves your computer**: the parts of files it reads and the output of commands go through the server to the model service.
**Browser access**: keep it off while you don’t use it, and use two-step verification while it is on.
blocks.p1: For the full notes, see [Safety notes](https://github.com/sun168567/cc-desk-tunnel#安全须知).

troubleshoot.title: Can’t connect
troubleshoot.lead: Read the first red line in the sign-in window: that is the reason.
troubleshoot.words: can’t connect connection failed certificate fingerprint credential token antivirus sshd execution channel proxy log

head: Message
What to do
rows: Connection timed out, refused, or the name can’t be resolved
Check the service address and port, and that the server is up and the port is open
Certificate not trusted, fingerprint doesn’t match
For a self-signed certificate, enter the SHA256 fingerprint given at install; enter it again if the server’s certificate changed
Check the token; after several failures in a row it is refused for a while
Upgrade one side as the message says
The SSH service couldn’t start, or was blocked
Most often antivirus software quarantined the bundled sshd.exe or PowerShell; look at its protection history first
When connecting through a proxy, make sure it allows several connections to the same address

blocks.p1: To find which part broke: “Open the log folder” in [About and updates](settings:about), and look at `client.log`. For more, see [Common problems and troubleshooting](https://github.com/sun168567/cc-desk-tunnel/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md).

faq.title: Questions
faq.lead: The questions that come up most in use.

faq1.q: Why does Claude keep running ssh?
a: That is how it works on your computer: Claude Code runs on the server and runs things on your computer through `ssh device-…`. See [How it works](#how-it-works).
Not whole. Claude reads files on your computer; the parts it reads and the output of commands go through the server to the model, as with Claude Code used locally.
The desktop client runs through the Agent SDK, which counts about twice as much against the 5-hour quota as the interactive CLI. Do long tasks in `ccdt`. See [Quota and usage](#quota).
After about an hour idle, the next message reads the context again at full price. Turning on auto compaction saves that. See [Cache and compaction](#context).

faq1.q: A task sits there and doesn’t move?
a: First see whether it is waiting for your approval or an answer. When the status dot says how long nothing has come, it only means no new messages in that time; long commands often do this.

faq1.q: What happens to a task when the computer sleeps or the network drops?
a: The task goes on on the server, and commands wait for the computer to come back. A task stops only after 5 minutes offline; when back, click “Continue”.

faq1.q: How do I get Claude to ask me less?
a: Use Auto approval; to have it change files directly but still ask before commands, use Accept edits. See [Approval modes](#approval).

faq1.q: Can’t start a session on another computer?
a: That computer must be online and have a project. Without one, have Claude go there from any session. See [Several computers](#devices#no-project).

faq1.q: Claude created files on the server?
a: That happens when the project is on your computer but the paths in the steps start with `/data/state/native/`. Tell it “do it on my computer instead”.

faq1.q: The quota or the model list is empty?
a: They come from a run of Claude Code: send a message, or refresh on the account page.

faq1.q: Two windows changing things in one folder at once?
a: You’re told when sessions of two connections run in the same folder at once; their changes may overwrite each other.
